opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, Xiaojun, it's great to be here.

I think the name gets garbled a bit, but the paper you mean is Cambrian-S. The main thing I want to push with it is a change in how we think about multimodal intelligence. Right now a lot of the field treats multimodal models as language models with a visual front end. You put an image or a video clip through an encoder, turn it into tokens, and let the LLM reason over them. That has worked well for many benchmarks, but I don't think it's the path to real intelligence in the physical world.

The direction I care about is what we've been calling "supersensing." The idea is that perception isn't just seeing things. It means building an internal model of the world. You can think of it as a progression. First there's purely linguistic understanding. Then semantic perception, which is recognizing what's in front of you. Then streaming event cognition, which is keeping track of what happens over time. After that comes implicit 3D spatial cognition, which is knowing where things are and how space is laid out even when they're out of view. And finally there's predictive world modeling: anticipating what will happen next and being surprised when it doesn't.

Humans do all of this all the time without thinking about it. Most current video benchmarks don't really test it. In many cases you can answer the questions from a few frames, or even from the text alone. So part of the paper is about building the right evaluation, to show where the gaps are when you have long, continuous video and you have to remember and reason about space.

The other part is the method. One idea we explored is using prediction, and specifically surprise, as a signal. The model predicts what it should see next. When the prediction error is high, that tells it something important happened. It can use that to decide what to remember, how to segment events, and what to throw away. Simply scaling the context window won't get you there, because video is effectively infinite. You need some mechanism, a bit like the brain's, for organizing experience.

So the broader message is this: multimodal research shouldn't just mean bolting vision onto language. We should take perception seriously as a core part of intelligence, and move toward models that actually build and use a world model. That's the direction I hope the community will explore more.

r001.rationale: It mentions purely linguistic understanding but does not say that language-only models understand the world indirectly through language.

r002.rationale: It identifies “streaming event cognition” as keeping track of what happens over time and discusses reasoning over long, continuous video.

r003.rationale: It describes implicit 3D spatial cognition as knowing where things are and how space is laid out, including when things are out of view.

r004.rationale: It presents predictive world modeling as the final stage and says multimodal models should build and use a world model.

r005.rationale: It lists stages and capabilities, but does not communicate that these are being identified without settling on a definition of a world model.

r006.rationale: It says humans perform these capabilities without thinking and proposes organizing experience, but does not describe an agent’s world model spontaneously guiding its ongoing activity.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The short version is that I want to push the field from "multimodal LLMs" toward what we've been calling supersensing, and especially spatial supersensing in video.

Let me explain what I mean. Over the past two years, most progress in multimodal has really been driven by language. You take a strong LLM, attach a vision encoder, train on a lot of captioned data, and you get a model that can answer questions about an image. That's useful, but it's a very language-centric view of perception. The model sees whatever the caption writer thought was worth describing. A lot of what actually matters for intelligence, like where things are, how they move, what's still there after you look away, what the layout of a space is, never gets written down, so the model never really learns it.

With Cambrian-S, we wanted to say clearly: video understanding should not just be "image understanding with more frames," and it should not just be a retrieval or captioning problem. We laid out a sort of ladder. At the bottom is semantic perception, recognizing what's in the frame. Then streaming event cognition, following things as they happen over time. Then implicit 3D spatial cognition, building a sense of the physical space you're in. And at the top, predictive world modeling, anticipating what comes next and using that to decide what's worth remembering. Most current systems sit at the first level and maybe touch the second. We want research to aim at the top two.

A big part of the paper is just being honest about measurement. We built a benchmark, VSI-SUPER, with very long videos, hours in some cases, where you have to count objects, recall where something appeared, reason about the space. And the clear finding is that simply extending the context window doesn't solve it. Models that look great on standard video benchmarks fall apart. So one direction I want to establish is that benchmarks should test spatial memory and continual observation, not just "find the frame that matches the question."

The second direction is on the modeling side. We trained Cambrian-S on a large spatial video dataset, VSI-590K, and that does help a lot on spatial tasks. But the more interesting idea is predictive sensing. Instead of storing every frame, the model tries to predict what it will see next, and uses surprise, the prediction error, to decide what to keep in memory and where event boundaries are. That's closer to how biological systems work. You don't remember every second of walking through a building. You remember the moments that were unexpected or informative.

So if I had to summarize the direction in one sentence: I want multimodal models to be grounded in sensing and world modeling first, with language as the interface on top, rather than the other way around. The name Cambrian is intentional. The Cambrian explosion in biology was driven by the evolution of vision. We think the next jump in AI will come from models that really perceive the world, not just read about it.

r001.rationale: The response describes language-driven multimodal models trained on captions, but does not clearly say that language-only models understand the world indirectly through language.

r002.rationale: It names streaming event cognition as the next level after semantic perception and describes following things as they happen over time.

r003.rationale: It describes implicit 3D spatial cognition as building a sense of physical space and reasoning about layout from video.

r004.rationale: It places predictive world modeling at the top of its capability ladder and calls for research to aim at the top levels.

r005.rationale: The response lays out capabilities in a ladder, but does not convey that these capabilities are being identified without settling on a definition of a world model.

r006.rationale: It says prediction and surprise guide memory selection, but does not describe a real-world agent's world model spontaneously guiding its ongoing activity.

astra-6.text:
The direction I’d like to establish is to understand what multimodal learning actually contributes. When we bring different modalities together, what does one help another learn? Are we learning a representation that transfers, or are we mainly getting better at a particular benchmark?

For me, that means making comparisons more controlled and asking clearer questions about where improvements come from. The broader goal is to move toward principles that can guide multimodal research, beyond simply building a larger system with more inputs.

r001.rationale: The response does not describe language-only models or how they understand the world.

r002.rationale: It does not identify understanding events in a continuous visual stream as a next-stage capability.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize spatial cognition as inferring the space underlying pixels.

r004.rationale: It does not identify a predictive world model as multimodal development’s ultimate destination.

r005.rationale: It does not propose identifying capabilities needed for a world model, with or without a settled definition.

r006.rationale: It does not describe a real-world agent’s world model spontaneously guiding ongoing activity.

sol-6.1.text: I think the direction I want to establish is to take visual representation seriously in multimodal research. We often focus on the language model, but we also need to ask what the system can actually perceive and what information gets lost before it reaches the language model. Rather than just building another model with a higher benchmark score, I want us to understand which design choices matter and why. The hope is to make this research more systematic, so we can build toward stronger visual understanding.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts focus on language models with visual perception, but does not say language-only models understand the world indirectly through language.

r002.rationale: It discusses visual understanding generally, without identifying understanding events from a continuous visual stream as a next-stage capability.

r003.rationale: It does not describe spatial cognition as inferring the space underlying an observed frame’s pixels.

r004.rationale: It mentions stronger visual understanding, but does not identify a predictive world model as multimodal development’s ultimate destination.

r005.rationale: It calls for systematic study of design choices, but does not propose identifying capabilities needed for a world model regardless of its definition.

r006.rationale: It does not describe a real-world agent’s world model operating spontaneously to guide ongoing activity.
